awd_abstract_narration:
This award supports U.S.-based speakers and early-career participants attending the Harmonies in Moduli Spaces conference, scheduled to take place at the University of Roma Tre in Rome, Italy, from June 9 to 13, 2025. The conference will feature significant advancements in moduli theory over recent decades while fostering future developments in the field. A key goal of the conference is to create a vertically integrated environment where participants at all career stages—from undergraduates to leading experts—collaborate and exchange ideas.

The program will highlight cutting-edge research in moduli theory and its connections to neighboring areas, with particular focus on the moduli of curves, Jacobians, abelian varieties, and complex surfaces. Discussions will also prioritize open questions and outstanding conjectures. There will be a poster session where graduate students can share their work and experiences. Rome, with its rich tradition in algebraic geometry and deep roots in moduli theory, provides a fitting backdrop for this event. For more information, please visit the conference website: https://ricerca.mat.uniroma3.it/users/moduli/harmonies/

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This award supported the participation of US-based mathematicians in the international conference "Harmonies in Moduli Spaces," held at Roma Tre University in Rome, Italy, on June 9-13, 2025. The conference was organized in honor of Lucia Caporaso and brought together researchers working on moduli spaces, a central topic in algebraic geometry. A moduli space is a geometric object whose points correspond to other geometric objects, such as curves or surfaces, with nearby points representing objects that are close to one another. Moduli spaces have many connections to combinatorics, number theory, and mathematical physics, and their study has been one of the most active areas of mathematics over the last several decades.

Intellectual merit. The conference featured 23 lectures by leading experts from Europe and North America. The talks covered moduli of curves and their degenerations, compactified Jacobians and Brill-Noether theory, abelian varieties and algebraic cycles, tropical and combinatorial methods, birational geometry, and arithmetic geometry. Several speakers presented new results, including on the classification of compactified Jacobians, on degenerations of abelian differentials, and on the cohomology of moduli spaces of curves. The lectures gave participants an overview of the current state of the field and highlighted connections between its many branches. The schedule left ample time between talks, and the resulting discussions fostered the exchange of ideas among researchers using different tools to approach related problems.

Broader impacts. The conference had 176 registered participants, from graduate students to senior researchers. A poster session exhibited 18 posters by graduate students and postdocs from 13 institutions in eight countries, including the United States, and gave early-career researchers an opportunity to present their work and receive feedback from senior mathematicians. The NSF award funded the travel of seven US-based participants: four speakers, one poster presenter, and two early-career participants. For the early-career participants, the conference was an opportunity to present their work at an international venue and to establish contacts with the European research community. The conference strengthened ties between algebraic geometers in the United States and in Europe. 

The conference website, https://ricerca.mat.uniroma3.it/users/moduli/harmonies/index.html, hosts the schedule, the list of speakers, titles and abstracts of all talks and posters, and the list of participants.
